Press Release:


Video game development is booming in South Africa and taking local programmers to the next level. What once used to be a very specialised industry overseas, has now moved closer to home with Cape Town becoming a hot-bed for emerging talent in the game industry. Some have already earned as much as a million rand in just one day. Carte Blanche meets independent young game makers upping their game to grow an industry that could be worth billions to the local economy.

Script:


GAME MAKERS SCRIPT
14/07/2015

PRODUCER: JAMES CARROLL

Opening: Desktop Dungeons winning at IGF AWARDS

JOHN LINK: The independent games industry breaks just about every business stereotype. This isn’t about people in suits and ties meeting in boardrooms or in office parks, it’s an industry that’s being driven by young people who are discussing things online or in nightclubs or even in kitchens.

KIDS PLAYING VIDEO GAMES

JOHN LINK: To the newcomer it’s a gathering that’s half-nightclub, half-games arcade but take a closer look and what you see represents a growing industry that could be worth billions of rands to the south African economy.

JOHN (VO): Capetonian Danny Day runs an established studio called QCF that experienced early success internationally with their game Desktop Dungeons.

Their game was entered into the Independent Games Festival where it was nominated for the grand prize and won excellence in design – no small feat considering its main competitor was Minecraft. Minecraft is an independent Swedish game that was sold to Microsoft for $2.5 billion in 2014.

JOHN: Do you think your success is sign of where we’re going in this country as far as independent developers are concerned?

DANNY DAY: One of the things that made me realize that I could be a game developer was watching how digital distribution was changing the industry. And seeing people from no matter where they were, in their bedrooms or on the other side of the world or whatever, as long as they had internet access they could release a game and people would buy it.

JOHN (VO): However this wasn’t the case initially. The fledgling company faced serious financial difficulties at first.

DANNY DAY: We ran out of cash in sort of May 2011. We got invited to E3, which is one of the biggest entertainment expos in the world. A chance to showcase our game there, no money to get there. And PayPal had launched the month before, in June. We said ‘okay let’s try this’. And we put the game up for pre-order as I climbed on a plane to get to LA. Got off the plane in LA, I could afford the trip. We could actually afford the next year’s worth of developments. So that was pretty cool.

JOHN (VO): Pretty cool indeed. Desktop Dungeons was released commercially in November 2013 but was actually profitable 5 months before its release.

JOHN (VO): According to industry body Make Games SA there are currently 40 active game development companies in the country with an estimated turnover of R53 million. While this may seem like a good start for a burgeoning industry, Nick Hall, a lawyer and founder of the organisation, explains this is just the beginning.

NICK HALL: The issue that we’re having now, I think, is a lack of skills. We’ve got companies now that are taking to the level where they need to start hiring and they want to ramp up, but there’s nobody with game development experience, which is actually quite a nice position to be in because we can say well there’s demand now. So if somebody wants to get into game design we can say ‘well yes, there’s jobs for you’.

JOHN (VO): Cape Town is becoming a hot-bed for emerging talent in the tech industry and the market is growing exponentially but far from the corporate offices in town is Free Lives, a studio in the leafy suburbs of Constantia that was founded by Evan Greenwood.

JOHN: Evan, walking into this house feels like walking into a completely different world – is that something you have a sense of, working in this environment?

EVAN GREENWOOD: I think there’s a lot about our lives that is unusual where we’re living in the same place we work, it’s this sort of ridiculous mansion at the moment which, that’s just the way things happened I guess.

JOHN (VO): Evan and the rest of his team are living communally while chasing to finish their independent game Broforce. From the outside the lifestyle may seem flexible but the work ethic is anything but.

EVAN: A lot of people I don’t think would be able to wrap their heads around quite what we’re doing here.

JOHN (VO): The needs of the artists and programmers are taken care of so they can devote all their time to the project. Meetings continue even during coffee breaks. And it’s good coffee too – running at a monthly cost of around R8000.

EVAN: We’re spending a lot of money here, but the reason is we knew we were getting to the end of a project, we knew that’s when a lot of the fun, creative decisions are already done and it’s now just pressure to finish something. We wanted to add as much comfort as we could then to those last few months.

JOHN: Let’s talk about the genesis of Broforce – where did the idea come from?

EVAN: We were busy with another game that possibly still could have been successful if we carried on, and there was like a game jam – like there’s these international gatherings of developers. They’re all working remotely but at the same time all around the world on making like a project on the weekend. Bro-force is all about these action heroes, and we were joking like ‘wouldn’t it be cool to have like Rambo in a game with like BA Baracus and like Chuck Norris and that kind of thing. It made sense to see just to see what would that actually do, we didn’t know. And then we made this thing and it’s kind of garbage, but it seemed like it was a good idea. I grew up with like Rambo and all of these action movies and it was a nice way to kind of relive that.

JOHN (VO): In order to fund this long development process, Broforce was released incomplete or “in early access” which enabled the team to connect with passionate fans who believed in the project and wanted to support them financially.

Broforce then attracted the attention of movie studios. Free Lives was approached to adapt their game and its motley crew of action heroes to tie in with the similarly themed movie the Expendables 3 creating Expendabros.

There have been more than 1.7 million downloads internationally and there is hot anticipation for the final release of Broforce.

EVAN: It started off with just working in our spare time, just two of us, and then like three people, four people and expanded from there. Anyway three years with eight people is still small in terms of what games are out there.

NICK HALL: Many South Africans don’t know that there is a local industry, because South Africa isn’t seen as a viable market for games.

DANNY DAY: We’ve had some wonderful things happen, like the 1st of January 2014 we went on a special sale on Steam and we made over a million Rand in one day, which is just amazing. And then we did that again in May and we made R1.4 million. So that’s sort of the spikes on this, how you earn things online, and learning to ride that and learning to understand that and sort of make it happen again and again and again is sort of, as a business person, that’s what we need to do.

NICK HALL: I do quite a lot of work with schools and sort of you hear kids they sort of see this and say ‘okay well I’m gonna quit school and make a game’, and they don’t appreciate sort of the effort that goes into it. And I think that’s something that we need to warn against; yes, you can make a successful industry, but it’s just going to require just as much work as anything else, you’re not guaranteed success.

JOHN LINK: In some cases independent games go on to make substantial amounts of money but that’s not always the primary concern. First and foremost for most of the developers it’s about finding a creative outlet.

JOHN VO: Cadence is Made with Monster Love’s music game and has been a personal journey for creator Peter Cardwell-Gardner.

PETER: For me the development of this game is really about overcoming my own challenges, overcoming my own artistic inhibitions. Making this game you invest yourself in it 100% so any successes the game has, any response the game has – you feel that personally, you feel as though people are responding to you, yourself which can be very challenging when it’s not what you expect.

EVAN: Being a creative field it does attract people who are more creatively inclined and there’s a little bit of like mental health kind of issues there. But I think in the same way that any creative field has and it’s not, this isn’t particularly unique to video games. It’s something I think we try and be very aware of, which I think it’s maybe more a case of it’s visible here because we tolerate it and we’re not going to try ostracize people like that.

It’s been a lot of like school of hard knocks, learning along the way. This is at our peak where we’re getting this game; it’s already kind of paid for itself, and that’s… I honestly thought I’d be at this point about 10 years ago; that was my plan getting out of high school, it just took a bit than I hoped. But I’m really happy I got here.
